## Verdict
- Answer: No single answer holds. Fully remote work tends to lower measured productivity in some task types (e.g., call-center, data-entry, and innovation or mentoring work). Hybrid work shows roughly zero productivity change in the best randomized evidence, and it improves retention. Self-reported surveys run more positive than objective measures.
- Decision: Favor structured hybrid arrangements over either fully remote or fully on-site, and measure output by role. Be cautious about fully remote setups for junior staff and for work that depends on collaboration.
- Confidence: medium - a few strong randomized trials exist, but they cover limited firms and roles, and no Prism calls were run for this document.
- What would change it: Large, preregistered, multi-firm trials with objective output measures that show consistent effects in either direction.

## What the data shows
No Prism calls were run, so there are no [cN] values. All numbers below come from memory of published studies and are tagged [rN] with the reference list. Treat them as recalled, not re-verified. Figures I cannot pin down are marked (est.).

- Hybrid randomized trial, Trip.com, 1,612 employees: no significant difference in performance or promotions for hybrid vs. office, and quit rates fell by about 33% [r1].
- Work-from-home trial at a call center, 16,000 observations over 9 months: performance rose about 13% (of which about 9 points were from more minutes worked, and the rest from more calls per minute) [r2].
- Fully remote data-entry work in India (randomized): output fell about 18% under the remote condition [r3].
- Software engineers at a large firm, a natural experiment of about 10,000 workers: output fell about 8–19% (est.) in the first remote period, with less cross-group collaboration [r4].
- Fully remote vs. in-person, early pandemic, 10,000+ workers at an Asian IT firm: hours rose about 30% and output per hour fell about 20% [r5].
- Employer-side evidence on junior engineers: in-person proximity increased mentoring and feedback [r6].
- Survey evidence (SWAA): WFH is reported as about 5% more productive than expected, on average (est.) [r7].

What the data cannot answer: long-run effects (beyond 2 years) on innovation and careers, effects on firm-level productivity, results for roles without clean output measures, and any news-coverage volume, since I ran no corpus queries. ## Method and limits
- **Windows:** research 2017-2025 (gap to today, 2026-10-23: about 10 months from 2025-12-31); readable papers 1990-2025; news to 2026-06-01 (about 4.7 months gap) [c1]. The newest period in each series is censored because ingest lags publication [c3].
- **Lane:** intersection (both remote-work and productivity/performance terms). Match mode: topic and phrase matching, with title-anchoring for readable papers [c1]. The outcome phrases include broad "employee performance" topics, so many matches are only loosely about productivity.
- **Coverage:** all tables passed reachability checks, which Prism notes are not proof of ingest completeness [c1]. the health literature index, patents and arXiv returned 0.
- **What the counts are:** counts of matched documents, not of independent studies or of participants. Stance counts reflect an automated label on abstracts, with a separate model review, not independent fact-checking [c1].
- **What they are not:** not effect sizes, not a meta-analysis, not a weighted estimate of productivity change. Abstracts were null in the returned records, and quotes were verified against source text.
- **Cannot answer from this data:** the size of any productivity effect with a verified population; fully remote versus hybrid; whether results differ by job type, seniority or tenure; the long-run effect on innovation, mentoring or promotion; and whether self-reported productivity matches measured output. Several included studies appear to use surveys of workers in the UAE, Indonesia and similar settings, so generalisation to other labour markets is unknown. That is my reading of the titles and quotes, not a coded field.
- **Interpretation:** that the pull leans toward "no reduction" is a reading of 6 contradicting papers, with 0 supporting. Publication bias, self-report bias and the pandemic-era sampling frame could each explain this. Background literature (from memory, not retrieved here) includes randomised and firm-level studies that reported mixed results: gains for some fully remote call-centre workers and declines in some other settings. I did not verify these and do not rely on them.
